definitions.meaning: The resultant force toward the centre of the circle that keeps an object in circular motion: F = mv^2/r. It is a role played by a real force such as tension, friction or gravity, not an extra force.
The acceleration toward the centre of the circle, a = v^2/r, caused by the changing direction of the velocity even when the speed is constant.
The attractive force between two masses given by Newton's law F = GMm/r^2, with G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2: double the separation and the force falls to one quarter.
A circular orbit above the equator, travelling west to east with period 24 hours, so the satellite stays fixed over one point on the equator.
The time for one complete orbit or revolution, T. For a circular orbit T = 2 pi r / v, and a geostationary period is exactly 24 hours.

mechanismSteps: Circular motion needs a centre-seeking push: a satellite stays on its circular path only because a force keeps pulling it towards the centre, and that force arrow always points at the centre wherever the satellite is.
How big is the centre-seeking force: the acceleration is a = v^2/r and the force is F = mv^2/r, so doubling the speed quadruples the force while doubling the radius halves it.
Gravity holds the Moon in orbit: Newton's law F = GMm/r^2 supplies exactly the centripetal force the Moon needs, so every orbit is a continuous fall towards the Earth that keeps missing it.

Geostationary orbits hover over one spot: with a period of exactly 24 hours above the equator and turning with the Earth, the satellite hangs motionless over one point while a drifting satellite falls behind.
Misconception: the fling-off force: there is no outward centrifugal fling - the body keeps going straight on the tangent while the seat pushes it inward, and that inward push is the real force.
objectives: Explain why circular motion needs a centripetal force toward the centre and compute it with F = mv^2/r
Use Newton's law of gravitation F = GMm/r^2 as the centripetal force for orbits
State the conditions for a geostationary orbit and avoid the centrifugal fling-off trap

trap.explanation: Being thrown sideways feels like an outward push. No outward fling exists: your body wants to keep going straight while the seat pushes you inward - the inward push is the real force. In the rotating car your inertia carries you along the tangent; the door and seat must push you inward to bend your path into the circle, and that inward push is the only horizontal force.
trap.misconception: A centrifugal force flings you outward in a sharp turn.

workedExample: A 0.50 kg ball whirled on a 1.2 m string at 6.0 m/s needs a centripetal force F = mv^2/r = 0.50 x (6.0)^2 / 1.2 = 0.50 x 36 / 1.2 = 15 N toward the centre, supplied by the string tension. Check the gravitation law the same way: for two 1.0 kg masses 1.0 m apart, F = GMm/r^2 = 6.67 x 10^-11 x 1.0 x 1.0 / 1.0^2 = 6.67 x 10^-11 N - tiny, which is why only planet-sized masses hold moons in orbit. Doubling the ball's speed to 12 m/s would quadruple the needed force to 60 N.
